column1: Why do we need distributed systems?
column2: We need them mainly for scaling, location, and fault-tolerance. They add complexity so they should be used when needed.;
Increasing system capacity either vertically with a stronger machine or horizontally with more machines.;
Scale up by using a stronger machine such as more memory or a faster CPU.;
Scale out by using more machines. It improves availability and fault-tolerance but adds complexity.;
Total speedup is limited by the part of work that cannot be parallelized.;
The number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles about every two years, historically increasing computing power over time.;
A high-end user's connection speed grows by about 50 percent per year.;
Disk density doubles about every 13 months.;
Software can get slower faster than hardware gets faster, because added complexity consumes hardware improvements.;
Systems can be placed closer to users to reduce latency or satisfy legal data-location requirements.;

Time To Live is decreased by each router. When it reaches zero, the router drops the packet and can send an ICMP Time Exceeded message.;
Message sent when a packet's TTL reaches zero. Traceroute uses this to discover intermediate routers.;
Content Delivery Network. Places content closer to users to reduce latency.;
Network latency has a physical lower bound because signals cannot travel faster than light.;
Fiber with one main light path. It has less delay spread and usually lower latency than multimode fiber.;
Fiber with many light paths. Some paths are longer, causing more delay spread.;
Different wavelengths of light travel at slightly different speeds in glass, which can affect latency.;
Fiber that guides light mostly through air, allowing signals to travel closer to vacuum speed.;
Preparing for failures so the system can continue despite individual hardware or network failures.;
Using multiple machines or replicas so another component can take over after a failure.;
Error-correcting memory that can correct one bit flip and detect two bit flips.;

SLC stores 1 bit per cell, MLC 2 bits, TLC 3 bits, and QLC 4 bits.;
More bits per NAND cell make storage cheaper and denser, but usually lower endurance and slower writes.;
Technique that spreads writes and erases across flash memory cells so they wear out more evenly.;

column1: What is the difference of VM / Container?
column2: A VM runs like a real computer with its own guest OS on a hypervisor. A container is an isolated user-space instance that shares the host OS/kernel.;
Docker packages software into containers. Containers are isolated with Linux mechanisms like network namespaces, cgroups, OverlayFS, seccomp profiles, and Linux capabilities.;

column1: What is docker-compose and how to run multiple services
column2: Docker Compose runs multiple containers together. Services are defined in docker-compose.yml and started as one application setup.;
Software that runs virtual machines. Type 1 runs on bare metal and Type 2 runs hosted on an operating system.;
Docker can use layered filesystems where image layers are shared and container changes are written to an upper layer.;
Docker can reuse an image layer if its input did not change, making repeated builds faster.;
Read-only base layer in OverlayFS, usually corresponding to Docker image layers.;
Writable layer in OverlayFS where new or changed container files are stored.;
Temporary working directory used internally by OverlayFS for file operations.;
Linux control groups limit and account resource usage such as CPU, memory, and I/O.;
Containers can use separate networks and communicate through configured container networks.;
Linux isolation mechanism that gives a process or container its own network environment.;
Virtual Ethernet device. It works like a virtual network cable between namespaces.;
Network Address Translation lets multiple devices share one public IP, but can make direct inbound connections harder.;
Technique where peers behind NAT coordinate packets to create mappings and enable direct communication.;
Keep images small and updated, scan vulnerabilities, avoid exposing the Docker daemon socket, avoid root, limit capabilities, and use read-only filesystems where possible.;

column1: What is a monorepo what is a polyrepo?
column2: A monorepo stores multiple project parts in one repository. A polyrepo splits a project across multiple repositories.;
Use monorepo for tightly connected projects with shared code or frequent joint changes. Use polyrepo for independent projects or separate teams and access control.;

column1: How do AI coding agents change the monorepo vs. polyrepo decision?
column2: Monorepos are easier for agents because related code is visible at once. Polyrepos need more setup and context management.;
One repository contains multiple parts of a project such as frontend and backend.;
A project is split across multiple repositories such as one repo for frontend and one for backend.;
Hardware, software, and cloud-based load balancers. Software load balancing can happen at L2/L3, L4, L7, DNS level, or with Anycast.;
It depends on control and use case. Hardware fits owned datacenters, cloud is pay-per-use, and software includes Traefik, Caddy, Nginx, HAProxy, MetalLB, DNS, and Anycast.;
Modern software reverse proxies such as Traefik, Caddy, Nginx, and HAProxy, plus cloud-based L4/L7 load balancers. Benchmark realistically.;

Like round-robin, but stronger servers receive a larger share of requests.;
Load balancer sends a request to the server with the fewest currently open requests.;
Peak exponentially weighted moving average. Load balancing algorithm that considers recent response latency.;
Sends the same user to the same backend, often with a cookie or source IP hash. Useful for stateful services but usually avoided.;
Mechanism for checking whether a backend is healthy before sending traffic to it.;
Load balancer sends probes, for example every few seconds, to check backend health.;
Load balancer infers backend health from real request failures.;
Separate API or control-plane check, useful when a TCP connection works but a dependency like a database is broken.;
Open-source software load balancer and reverse proxy written in Go, with L4/L7 support, HTTP/3 support, and a dashboard.;
Open-source L7 reverse proxy and static file server with automatic HTTPS through Let's Encrypt.;
Fast web server, reverse proxy, mail proxy, and load balancer. It commonly uses passive health behavior.;

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. Browsers restrict cross-origin HTTP requests from scripts.;

column1: Explain what MCP is why it exists and how tool calling works (tools/list tools/call JSON-RPC)
column2: MCP is an open protocol by Anthropic that connects AI agents to external tools, data sources, and services. tools/list asks what tools exist and tools/call runs one.;

column1: Describe the MCP message flow between user client LLM and MCP server
column2: The flow is user to assistant tool_call to tool result to assistant answer. Tool results must include the correct tool_call_id.;

column1: Discuss challenges of running MCP in the browser and how WebMCP addresses them
column2: Browsers can block or limit external fetching. WebMCP can use browser-side tools such as an extension that injects client_web_search and acts like an MCP server.;

column1: What authentication mechanisms exists for web applications?
column2: Passwords, MFA/2FA, TOTP, Basic Auth, Digest Auth, mTLS, session-based auth, JWT access and refresh tokens, and OAuth.;

column1: How can stateless authentication be achieved?
column2: With JWTs. The server signs a token after login and the client sends it with Authorization Bearer token. Servers verify it without remembering a session.;
The client sends username and password in an HTTP request. It should use HTTPS because Base64 is encoding not security.;
Uses hash and nonce for replay protection. Password is not sent in clear text but password storage options are limited.;
Both sides verify each other. The client checks the server and the server checks the client certificate.;
A JSON-based access token with header payload and signature.;
Short-lived token such as 10 minutes. It can contain userId, role, and other trusted information.;
Longer-lived token used to get a new access token from the auth server.;
Authorization for third party integrations without giving away passwords.;
OAuth variant for clients that cannot safely store a client secret such as mobile apps or SPAs.;

Things developers often assume about networks but should not assume.;
The network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous.;
Network layers provide services to the layer above. Protocols let entities at the same layer on different hosts communicate.;
TCP is reliable and ordered. It uses retransmission, sequence numbers, ACKs, checksums, flow control, and congestion control.;

column1: What are the problems of TCP and how other protocols (HTTP/3) can improve that
column2: TCP can require multiple round trips, and ordered delivery can delay everything. HTTP/3 uses QUIC with faster handshakes, built-in security, and multiplexing.;
Protocol data unit. It contains a protocol header and payload called the SDU.;
SYN SYN-ACK ACK establishes a TCP connection.;
If no ACK is received after a timeout TCP resends data.;
Three duplicate ACKs can trigger retransmission of missing packets.;
Prevents the sender from overwhelming the receiver by using a sliding window.;
TCP mechanisms such as slow-start and congestion avoidance reduce network overload.;
Transport Layer Security. It uses client hello, server hello, key exchange, and finished messages.;
Transport protocol used by HTTP/3 with 1 RTT handshake, built-in security, and multiplexing.;
Connectionless communication with no guarantee of delivery, ordering, or duplicate protection.;
Message-based transport protocol with multiple streams and multi-homing but not widely used.;
UDP services can be abused to send larger spoofed responses to a victim.;

column1: Overview over important protocols on layer 7
column2: Important application protocols include HTTP, WebSockets, Server Sent Events, WebRTC, DNS, Let's Encrypt/ACME, and mail protocols such as SMTP, POP, and IMAP.;

column1: Custom protocols ASN.1 RPC HTTP JSON WebSockets Server Sent Events
column2: Custom protocols can be efficient but harder to build, test, debug, document, and keep compatible. ASN.1 is used for certs. RPC runs code remotely. HTTP transports data. JSON is a data format. WebSockets and SSE support browser communication.;

column2: WebRTC enables browser P2P communication. DNS maps names to IPs. Let's Encrypt automates TLS certificates. Mail protocols include SMTP, POP, and IMAP.;

column1: Why does scaling lead to consensus problems?
column2: Scaling means multiple components or servers. Unreliable components and replicas can create inconsistent state so the system needs consensus.;

column1: Fault models: crash faults vs. Byzantine faults
column2: Crash faults mean a component fails or becomes unavailable. Byzantine faults mean arbitrary behavior such as lying for advantage.;
Paxos chooses a single value if a majority is available. Raft uses followers, candidates, and one leader with elections and heartbeats.;
vDHT uses no locking or timestamps. Every update creates a new version and conflicts may need manual resolution.;
CRDTs avoid leaders and majorities and can work during partitions but only for suitable data structures.;
Paxos/Raft need majority or leader. vDHT may need app conflict resolution. CRDTs avoid leaders but need suitable merge logic.;

column1: Understand how Bitcoin works as a peer-to-peer system
column2: Bitcoin has no central bank. Transactions are created by peers and broadcast to the whole network.;

column1: Get familiar with UTXO mining and proof-of-work
column2: Coins are spent as whole UTXO pieces while miners create valid blocks by solving proof-of-work puzzles.;

column1: Be aware of risks like the 51% attack
column2: An attacker with more than 50 percent computing power could influence transaction ordering and exclude transactions.;

column1: Reflect on advantages and disadvantages of Bitcoin
column2: Bitcoin is decentralized and can have low fees and strong anonymity but has high power use volatility and scalability limits.;
Unspent transaction output. Bitcoin spends coins as whole pieces and returns change as a new output.;
